maths_errors.text: When it does factorise, find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, then write the two brackets.
maths_errors.correction: This only works directly when a = 1, where ac = c and the brackets are (x + p)(x + q). When a ≠ 1 the two numbers cannot just be placed in brackets. Example: 2x² + 7x + 3 has ac = 6, so the numbers are 1 and 6, but the answer is not (x + 1)(x + 6). Use the numbers to split the middle term: 2x² + x + 6x + 3 = x(2x + 1) + 3(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)(x + 3).

maths_errors.text: Always check solutions by substituting back into the original equation. Both values must make the equation equal zero.
maths_errors.correction: A repeated root has only one value to check. Formula answers rounded to decimal places give only approximately zero when substituted back, not exactly zero. Example: x² + 4x + 1 = 0 gives x ≈ −0.27 or x ≈ −3.73. Substituting x = −0.27 gives about 0.0029. The fact should say exact solutions give 0 and rounded solutions give a value close to 0.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: factorising quadratic expressions of the form x ^2 + bx + c , including the difference of two squares
missing_spec_content.why: The difference of two squares (e.g. x² − 49 = (x + 7)(x − 7)) is never taught or mentioned.
Expanding (x + p)(x + q) is not taught. It is also not used to check the factorised form.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Higher only: expanding products of two or more binomials • factorising quadratic expressions of the form ax ^2 + bx + c
missing_spec_content.why: Factorising when a ≠ 1 is only hinted at in one incorrect sentence. Expanding three binomials is absent.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions (including those involving surds
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never shows how to write quadratic formula answers in simplified surd form.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Basic foundation: collecting like terms • multiplying a single term over a bracket • taking out common factors • simplifying expressions involving sums, products and powers, including the laws of indices
missing_spec_content.why: None of this basic manipulation is taught. In particular, taking out a common factor (e.g. x² − 5x = x(x − 5)) is a standard way to solve quadratics with c = 0 and is not covered.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: identify and interpret roots, intercepts and turning points of quadratic functions graphically
missing_spec_content.why: Graphs of quadratics, roots as x-intercepts, the y-intercept and turning points are not covered.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Notes: including the symmetrical property of a quadratic
missing_spec_content.why: The line of symmetry of a parabola is not mentioned.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Higher only: deduce turning points by completing the square
missing_spec_content.why: Completing the square and reading off the turning point are absent.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: find approximate solutions using a graph
missing_spec_content.why: Solving a quadratic by reading a graph is not taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Higher only: including those that require rearrangement including completing the square
missing_spec_content.why: Neither rearranging to the form ax² + bx + c = 0 nor solving by completing the square is taught.

cases_not_modelled.why: The formula is stated but never fully worked through, and there is no example with a non-integer or decimal-place answer.

cases_not_modelled.case: Negative b and/or negative c (e.g. x² − x − 12 = 0)
cases_not_modelled.why: The only example has both coefficients positive, so the sign rules for mixed-sign factor pairs are never shown.
This is required at Foundation and has no example.
There is no example of factorising out x, which gives the root x = 0.

No example starts in a form other than ax² + bx + c = 0.
There is no example of writing (x + p)² + q, solving with it or finding a turning point.
No example reads roots from a parabola.
The discriminant cases are described, but no example shows a zero or negative discriminant.

density.text: b² − 4ac is called the discriminant: if it is positive there are two solutions, zero gives one repeated solution, and negative means no real solutions.
density.why: One sentence introduces a new term and three cases. It does not explain why: the discriminant sits under the square root, and ± adds or subtracts it.

density.text: When it does factorise, find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, then write the two brackets.
density.why: A whole second method is squeezed into the end of the formula explanation with no example. It also says 'ac', while the worked example uses 'the constant'.

density.text: They appear in geometry (area equations), physics (projectile motion), and many Higher-tier problems — learning to factorise and apply the quadratic formula covers the vast majority of exam questions.
density.why: This long sentence carries several ideas and names two methods before either is explained.

density.text: Find two numbers that multiply to +6 (the constant) and add to +5 (the coefficient of x).
density.why: The reason is not given. Expanding (x + p)(x + q) = x² + (p + q)x + pq is what makes this work.

density.text: Write them as (x + p)(x + q) = 0, then solve x = −p and x = −q.
density.why: The step to x = −p is given without saying that one bracket must equal zero because the product is zero.

density.text: Substituting into the quadratic formula with the wrong sign for b — e.g. for x² + 5x + 6 = 0, using b = +5 in the −b term of the formula to get (5 ± √1)/2 instead of using −b = −5 to get (−5 ± 1)/2.
density.why: This is the first time the formula is applied in the lesson, and it appears inside a mistake. The √1 comes from 25 − 24 without that being shown.
